reason: The provided sources do not mention the mission-ending near-miss involving rocket vibrations minutes after lift-off, and other glitches like the 1978 radio failure lack the 10-claim, two-site depth required to tell that specific story.
story: In 1977, NASA launched Voyager 2 on a mission that officially was not supposed to happen. A rare celestial alignment, occurring only once every 175 years, offered a 'Grand Tour' of all four outer planets. However, Congress canceled the project due to costs, scaling it back to a simple visit to Jupiter and Saturn. But mission designers chose a trajectory that kept the dream alive. Launching on August 20, 1977, atop a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket, Voyager 2 left Earth 16 days before its twin. Though its primary radio receiver failed just months later in April 1978, the probe utilized its backup and successfully visited Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—becoming the only spacecraft in history to reach the ice giants. Today, over 45 years after launch, the probe is in interstellar space, carrying a Golden Record of Earth's sounds into the eternal void.
angle: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit the ice giants Uranus and Neptune, reaching them only because of a planetary alignment that happens once every 175 years.

claims.claim: The four largest outer planets aligned in a rare celestial arc during the late 1970s.
Gary Flandro discovered that this alignment occurred only once every 175 to 176 years.
Using gravity assists allowed a probe to cut travel time to Neptune from 30 years down to 12.
The original 'Grand Tour' plan was canceled in 1971 due to high estimated costs.
Voyager 2 launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on August 20, 1977.
The spacecraft was launched atop a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket.
Voyager 2 launched 16 days before its twin, Voyager 1.
Voyager 1 took a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter four months before Voyager 2.
The mission mission was originally planned to last only four years.
Voyager 2's primary radio receiver failed in April 1978, months after launch.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited the ice giants Uranus and Neptune.
During its flyby of Uranus, Voyager 2 discovered 11 previously unknown moons.
The spacecraft officially entered the interstellar medium on November 5, 2018.
Both Voyager probes carry a golden record intended as a message for extraterrestrial life.
The spacecraft are powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators using Plutonium-238.
